titre: The Word Invented Because the Crime Had No Name
accroche: In 1944, a Polish jurist who had taken refuge in the United States coins a word. Without it, there was no name for what he was describing.
contenu_vulgarise:
November 1944, Washington. The Carnegie Endowment for International Peace publishes a thick, technical book, “Axis Rule in Occupied Europe,” by a Polish jurist who had taken refuge in the United States, Raphael Lemkin. The book is first of all a work of compilation: it gathers and analyzes the decrees by which Germany and its allies administer the territories they occupy. In chapter nine, Lemkin pauses and coins a word, because he finds that he lacks one.

## A compound, and why it was needed

The word is built from two pieces: the Greek genos, meaning family, tribe, race, and the Latin suffix cide, from caedere, to kill. Genocide. The chapter is, literally, titled “A New Term and New Conception for Destruction of Nations.”

Lemkin insists on a point that the word has since partly lost. Genocide, he writes, does not necessarily mean the immediate destruction of a nation. It refers to a coordinated plan of different actions aimed at destroying the essential foundations of the life of national groups: their political and social institutions, their culture, their language, their religion, their economic existence. Mass murder is its most visible expression, not its definition.

The need for the word was legal before it was moral. The international law of the day knew war crimes, committed by one belligerent against another. It could not name what a state does to a population, including its own, outside of any combat. An act without a name is an act without a legal characterization, and an act without a legal characterization cannot be prosecuted. Lemkin had already run into this gap in 1933, when he presented to an international criminal law conference in Madrid a proposal targeting a crime he then called barbarity.

## What a word does once it exists

The term is taken up as early as the Nuremberg trials, then enters positive law: on December 9, 1948, the United Nations adopts the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, several provisions of which come from Lemkin's proposals.

Four years separate the coining of the word from its entry into an international treaty. That is very short, and it says something about how law works. The convention did not make criminal a behavior that was not already so; it gave a name to something that no one could prosecute for lack of a way to designate it. The word did not follow the rule, it made the rule possible.

Lemkin lost almost his entire family to what he had named. He spent the rest of his life getting the convention ratified, country by country.

repere.texte: The word genocide first appears in November 1944, in chapter IX of “Axis Rule in Occupied Europe.” The international convention that punishes it is adopted four years later, on December 9, 1948.
repere.source: Raphael Lemkin, Axis Rule in Occupied Europe, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 1944, chapter IX

carte.punch: An act without a name is an act without a legal characterization. And an act without a legal characterization cannot be prosecuted.
carte.idee: In 1944, the jurist Raphael Lemkin coins the word genocide, from the Greek genos and the Latin cide, because international law had no way to name what a state does to an entire population. Four years later, the UN adopts a convention to punish it.
carte.source_courte: Lemkin, Axis Rule in Occupied Europe, 1944

quiz.question: According to the definition Lemkin gives of the word he coins in 1944, what does genocide refer to?
choix: The immediate, massive killing of the members of a group, the only case he meant to cover
Any war crime committed by an occupying army against civilians
A coordinated plan to destroy the foundations of a group's life, of which killing is only one expression
The organized deportation of a population out of its territory of origin
quiz.explication: Lemkin writes explicitly that genocide does not necessarily mean the immediate destruction of a nation, but a coordinated plan of different actions aimed at a group's political and social institutions, culture, language, religion and economic existence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the book “Axis Rule in Occupied Europe,” published in 1944, mainly gather?
choix: The decrees by which Germany and its allies administer the occupied territories
The transcripts of the Nuremberg trials of Nazi leaders
The preparatory debates for the 1948 convention at the United Nations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The book is first of all a work of compilation that gathers and analyzes the occupation decrees, before Lemkin coins the word genocide in chapter nine.

quiz_supplementaire.question: From what linguistic roots is the word “genocide” formed?
choix: From the Latin genus and the Greek thanatos
From the Greek genos and the Greek nomos
From the Greek genos and the Latin cide
From the Latin gens and the German mord
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lemkin forms the word from the Greek genos, meaning family, tribe or race, and the Latin suffix cide, from caedere, to kill.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Lemkin call, in 1933, the crime he was trying to get recognized at a criminal law conference in Madrid?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1933 in Madrid, Lemkin had presented a proposal targeting a crime he then called barbarity, eleven years before coining the word genocide.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what did the 1948 convention concretely change compared with the earlier situation?
choix: It replaced the notion of war crime with that of genocide
It entrusted the judging of genocides to a permanent tribunal
It made criminal a behavior that had not been so before
It named what no one could prosecute for lack of a way to designate it
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the convention did not make a novel behavior criminal, but gave a name to what could not be prosecuted without a way to designate it.
